body.text: Permanent outdoor lights (also called permanent holiday lights, soffit track lights, or architectural roofline lighting) are individually addressable RGBW LED pucks recessed into an aluminum track that mounts under your soffit or along your fascia. Once installed they stay up year-round, controlled from your phone, and can produce warm white for everyday use, colour scenes for holidays, or dynamic effects for game nights. The obvious question before you commit is the honest one: what does this actually cost in Canada in 2026? Below we break down what drives the price on both routes, buying a DIY kit and installing it yourself or having it professionally installed, and where to find current figures.
The two ways to buy, and why prices differ so much

Almost every quote you will see falls into one of two buckets. A DIY kit is the hardware only: the LED pucks, aluminum track, a WiFi controller, a power supply, connectors and mounting screws, shipped to your door for you to install on a weekend. A professional install is that same class of hardware plus labour, ladders, layout planning, wiring, and cleanup, priced by the linear foot and installed by a crew. The gap between the two is almost entirely labour and the installer's hardware markup, which is why a DIY kit costs less than a turnkey job for the same size of home.

Rule of thumb: measure your roofline in linear feet first. Everything else about pricing, from kit size to an installed quote, keys off that one number. Most two-storey Canadian homes land somewhere between 120 and 200 linear feet of coverable roofline.
DIY kit sizes and what sets the price

Our DIY kits are sold as complete track lighting kits sized by linear footage, so you buy roughly the length you need and add a little margin for corners and offcuts. There are six sizes: 50, 75, 100, 150, 200 and 250 ft. Each includes the pucks, track, controller and power supply, and kits of 100 ft and up also include power injection parts and a data amplifier. Footage is what sets the price, so the first step is matching a size to your home:

items: 50 or 75 ft kit: small bungalow front, garage, or a single feature elevation
100 ft kit: typical single-storey home or a modest two-storey front
150 ft kit: average two-storey home, front plus partial sides
200 or 250 ft kit: larger two-storey, wraparound coverage

body.text: These are complete, warrantied kits rather than bargain-bin strip lights. Cheaper spools of generic LED tape exist, but they are not the same product: they lack individually addressable pucks, weather-rated aluminum track, and the controllers that make year-round Canadian outdoor use reliable. Our prices change from time to time, so see current kit prices at /diy-kits, where you can also see what is in each kit.
Buying individual parts instead of a full kit

If you are extending an existing run, replacing a component, or building a non-standard layout, buying parts individually is often the smarter spend. Every part is listed with its current price at /shop; these are the pieces that make up a run:

items: 12V RGBW LED pucks: the lights themselves, which make up the bulk of any kit's cost
Aluminum track (available in four soffit colours to blend in)
WiFi controller: runs colours, scenes and schedules from the app
Power supply (60W to 300W): sized to the number of pucks on the circuit
Connectors, power-injection cables and amplifiers: needed on longer runs to keep colour and brightness even

body.text: The reason we call out power injection and amplifiers is that they are the parts most first-timers forget. Long single runs lose voltage toward the far end, which shows up as dimming or colour shift. Injecting power partway along the run, or adding an amplifier, fixes it. You can browse every component on the shop page and match colours and wattages to your layout.
Professional installation pricing

If you would rather not be on a ladder, professional installation is priced per linear foot installed, hardware included. For our own installs, see /installation for installed pricing; the quote depends on your footage, how many storeys the home has, and how many separate runs the roofline needs.

For context on what dealer-only brands charge, Trimlight publishes $18 to $35 a foot installed and Jellyfish $25 to $35 a foot installed (both are US companies that do not state a currency), while Gemstone and Celebright do not publish prices. The full comparison is at /brands.

We now offer professional installation across Southwestern Ontario, covering London, Woodstock, and the Kitchener-Waterloo region. For local homeowners that means one crew handles measurement, layout, mounting, wiring, and cleanup, and you get the same 5-year parts warranty on the hardware. If you are outside that area, the DIY kit ships free to any address in Canada and is designed to be installed with basic tools in a weekend. You can request a local quote on the installation page.
What actually drives your cost
Two homes on the same street can get very different quotes. Here is what moves the number, roughly in order of impact:

items: Linear footage: the number one factor for both DIY and installed pricing, because it sets how many pucks and how much track you need.
Home height and access: two- and three-storey homes, steep rooflines, or hard-to-reach peaks add labour time and safety equipment to an installed quote.
Number of runs and power injections: complex layouts with several separate sections need extra controllers, injections, or amplifiers.
DIY versus installed: the hardware is the same either way; an installed quote adds the labour, ladders and layout work on top.
Soffit condition and colour matching: choosing a track colour to match your soffit is free, but damaged or unusually deep soffits can add labour.
Controller and feature level: single-zone versus multi-zone control and app features nudge the hardware price.
Region and season: installer rates vary by market, and booking in the busy autumn run-up to the holidays can cost more than the off-season.

body.text: Watch out for quotes priced only 'per home' with no linear-foot breakdown. Ask for the footage and the per-foot rate so you can compare apples to apples, and confirm the warranty length and whether returns are supported.
Is permanent lighting worth it versus temporary lights?

Permanent lighting is a larger one-time cost, but it replaces a recurring one. Buying and replacing temporary light strings, plus paying a service to hang and remove them each year, adds up quickly. In many Canadian markets a professional hang-and-remove alone runs several hundred dollars every season, before you count damaged strings and storage. A permanent system removes that annual bill and gives you everyday architectural lighting, holiday colour, and security lighting from a single install. For most homeowners the payback lands within a few seasons, and DIY shortens that further by removing labour cost entirely.
So, what should you budget?

For a realistic 2026 plan, start by measuring your roofline: that single number tells you which kit size to look at and gives any installer the basis for an honest quote.
